| Field | |
|---|---|
| **Year** | Preprint posted 6 June 2025. Peer reviewed version in *Genome Biology*, April 2026 |
| **Models** | **Human, chimpanzee and rhesus macaque**, compared pairwise against human. Four individuals per species. No mouse |
| **Brain region** | **None.** The tissues are heart (left ventricle), kidney cortex, liver and lung |
| **Measures** | **RNA.** But the method is written for any read-based measure: chromatin accessibility, binding, splicing |
| **Method** | **Bulk RNA-seq**, 50 bp single-end, 48 samples, reused from the group's earlier study. Plus **simulated** RNA-seq with known differences planted in 10% of genes |
| **Cross-species stats** | Reads aligned with STAR, keeping uniquely mapped reads only. Reciprocal liftover through UCSC chains. Orthologous features from the **Comparative Annotation Toolkit (CAT)**. Differential expression with edgeR and limma-voom, FDR ≤ 5%. Compared against five other pipelines |

## My reading

For the literature review I found one more very interesting paper, which fits exactly with
our to-do, which is the CrossFilt paper. It is a preprint, which means that it has not been, I
think, admitted to a journal yet, and probably has not undergone a peer review process. Which
until this point, I think is fine.

What essentially they are doing, or what they have built, is **CrossFilt**. CrossFilt is a
**filtering strategy that retains only sequencing reads that map between genomic features**. I
think on the same side. What it does is it **aligns sequencing reads to a reference genome**,
then it identifies **orthologues and syntenic genomic features**, and it counters **alignment
bias**, which is interspecies variation in length etc., by just keeping the reads between the
genomic features that can be found definitely in both genomic datasets.

They do discuss the **genome annotation quality** between species, but for the species that I
have in mind, human, macaque and mouse, that should not be a huge issue.

In this paper they applied CrossFilt to **RNA sequencing data from humans, chimpanzee and
rhesus macaque**, so up until this point I do not know whether you can use it for different
datasets. Maybe you can, since it relies on genomic data, so that you can map it. I guess RNA
data is pretty useful for **enrichment**, because that is what Miao and others have done this
year, 2026, in the paper that we have.

CrossFilt also **reduces the number of false positives**, which is amazing.

**How does it work?** This is what I currently have. I have not read through the whole paper.

1. It aligns sequencing reads derived from target samples to the target reference genome.
2. Then CrossFilt uses the reference genome coordinates to identify the start and end
   positions.
3. It retrieves all **chains**. I do not know what that is yet. If there are more chains, it
   selects the chain with the highest **UCSC score**, which reflects length and quality of
   alignment, favouring long gap-free regions.
4. Then it **lifts** the reads, transforms them into **FASTQ** format, and independently
   realigns them to the query genome using the query species annotations. So I suppose that
   the genes kind of overlap, so that if you run the computation you have both sides, I think.
5. For the orthologues they use the **Comparative Annotation Toolkit, CAT**, which keeps only
   reads that map consistently to the same genomic feature in both species. So at this point I
   believe there is not a **one-to-many orthologue** system, because you are cutting them out.

## What I take from it

It fits exactly with our to-do. It reduces the number of false positives, which is amazing,
and at this point there is not a one-to-many orthologue system, because you are cutting them
out.

## Checks against the paper

- **It has now been peer reviewed.** The preprint was published in *Genome Biology* in April
  2026 (volume 27, article 187). Cite the journal version from now on.
- **"Map between genomic features, I think on the same side."** Each read is carried to the
  other species' genome, realigned there, and carried back. It is kept only if it lands in
  exactly the same place both ways.
- **What a chain is.** A run of alignment blocks between two genomes, kept in the same order in
  both, with no duplications or inversions. It is the bridge the read is lifted across.
- **On one-to-many orthologues, you are right.** Only uniquely mapped reads are kept, and
  chains exclude duplications, so duplicated genes are cut out.
- **Annotation quality.** The paper names human and mouse as the well curated annotations.
  Macaque is in the less curated group, which is why they transfer the human annotation onto
  it with CAT.
- **Different datasets.** Only primates were tested, not mouse. The authors say it should
  extend to more distant species and to other read based data, but do not show it.

## Open questions from this read

- Has anyone run CrossFilt on **human vs mouse**, and how many reads survive at that distance?
- Does it work on **single-cell or single-nucleus** data, where reads are short and come with
  cell barcodes? Every result here is bulk.
- How did **Miao 2026** align their reads? If each species went to its own genome and genes
  were matched as orthologue pairs afterwards, that is close to what this paper calls
  dual-reference, the approach with the worst false positive rate.
- They found a spurious "cytoplasmic translation" signal driven by ribosomal genes with
  near-identical sequence. Miao **excluded ribosomal genes** outright. Same problem, two
  different fixes?

## How it relates to this project

1. **It is a ready-made algorithm for the method-driven pipeline.** The to-do on the home page
   is to rebuild the pipeline on established algorithms for each step. CrossFilt is one for
   the expression side: deciding which genes are BBB-enriched before conservation is ever
   measured. That step currently comes from Wälchli and is checked against Miao.

2. **It does not touch the conservation step itself.** This project compares **coding
   sequence**, not reads. Percent identity and dN/dS come from aligned CDS, so read mapping
   bias does not enter there. CrossFilt matters wherever the project uses expression data to
   choose or validate genes.

3. **It agrees with the one-to-one decision.** Its own design cuts out duplicated regions, the
   same way Miao restricted to one-to-one orthologues. That is now three lines of support
   for applying the [`step5d`](../audit.qmd) fix to the BBB set as well as the control.

4. **It is a warning about any expression comparison the project adds.** The macaque
   expression atlas in [Extensions](../extensions.qmd) would mean comparing expression across
   species. If that is done by aligning each species to its own genome and matching genes by
   name, this paper says to expect a lot of false differences.

## Reference detail from the paper

- **Data.** 48 bulk RNA-seq samples: 4 individuals × 4 tissues × 3 species. SRA accessions
  SRR6900765 to SRR6900812. Genomes hg38, panTro6, rheMac10; human annotation from Ensembl
  v110.
- **Simulation.** 34,693 genes for human vs chimpanzee, 31,807 for human vs macaque. 10% made
  differentially expressed at log fold change 2, half each direction.
- **Empirical FDR on simulated data.** CrossFilt 4.0% and 4.0%. Consensus 5.4% and 8.9%.
  Single-reference 6.8% and 18.5%. Orthologous exons 10.9%. Annotation transfer 12.0%.
  Dual-reference 53% and 57%. (Human vs chimpanzee, then human vs macaque.)
- **Real data.** 68.2% of the differentially expressed genes found only by dual-reference
  were found by no other method. Fewer than half of DE genes were found by every approach.
- **Code.** <https://github.com/kennethabarr/CrossFilt>
